name: Carla Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Carla, thanks for doing this. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything here is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a junior buyer at a wholesaler that sells shampoo, skincare and cosmetics to pharmacies and beauty salons. I buy mostly from factories in Italy and South Korea, so my day starts with Korean emails that came in overnight and ends with Italian ones. I use an AI assistant for nearly everything: translating, summarising price lists, drafting replies, even checking ingredients against the import rules.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The actual judgment. The AI can tell me a serum is cheaper from one factory, but my boss Ingrid knows which factory ships late every summer. I've made a couple of expensive calls already, like four thousand units of a sunscreen that didn't sell. Ingrid was kind about it, but I felt it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a studio near the river, which I love. I've got about five months of costs put away. On weekends I sell vintage clothes online, which makes maybe two hundred a month, more for fun than money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a good assistant, not a boss, which is what I've always thought. I'd probably post a little thread about how I actually use it, the boring practical stuff. At work I'd keep doing what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be fine, maybe better than fine. I'm the junior who already squeezes the most out of the tools, so I'd be the one they give more ranges to. The only thing that worries me is the sunscreen kind of mistake, which is about my judgment, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and ask Ingrid for the Korean skincare range on my own, which is the fastest-growing one. I'd do a short course on import regulations so I stop leaning on the AI for that. And I'd keep the vintage selling going, maybe push it to four hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit restless, actually, because I like change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why restless?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a world where nothing much changes is a world where I wait five years to get promoted. Ingrid's been a buyer for nine years. I'd want to move faster than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with that restlessness?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably put more time into the vintage shop, or look at a buyer job at a bigger chain where things move quicker. There are a few nearby. I'm not desperate, I'd just keep my eyes open.

say: I'd say AI is a good **assistant**, not a **boss**.
I'd post a practical **thread** on how I actually use it at work.
think: I'm the junior who already **squeezes the tools** hardest, so I'd get more ranges.
My real weak spot is **judgment**, like the unsold sunscreen order.
do: Ask Ingrid for the **Korean skincare range**, the fastest-growing one.
Take a short **import regulations** course to stop relying on AI for it.
Grow the **vintage shop** to about four hundred a month.
feel: **Calm**, with a little **restlessness** because she likes change.
S0.quote: A world where nothing much changes is a world where I wait five years to get promoted.
fieldNote: She owns her **sunscreen mistake** and frames her weakness as judgment, not tech.
Her AI Plateau worry is **slow promotion**, not job loss.
The **vintage side-business** is small but shows a habit of trying things.

steps.text: Ask Ingrid to give her the Korean skincare range
Take a short course on cosmetics import regulations
Grow the vintage clothes shop to four hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so learn the tools or get left behind, but I'd say it kindly. I don't think it's anyone's fault, it's just what businesses do when something's cheaper. At work I'd offer to help set up whatever system they choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think buying teams shrink a lot, and juniors are exposed. But I'm the junior who's basically doing the new job already. I'd want to be the one who checks the system's orders, not the one it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd ask to run a trial where the AI drafts all supplier orders for my range and I just approve them. I'd keep a log of where it gets things wrong, to show Ingrid I add something. And I'd start applying for buyer jobs at bigger chains, where there'll be more of these roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but a lot of excitement mixed in. I'd rather be at the front of this than the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd run a trial that could make your own role smaller. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if I don't run the AI ordering trial, someone in head office will, and they'll do it without me. If I run it, I'm the person who knows how it fails. That's worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ingrid, oddly. She's brilliant at the relationships, but she hates screens and she's forty-eight. If the firm decides relationships don't matter, she's in trouble, and I'd lose my best teacher.

say: I'd say **learn the tools** or get left behind, but say it kindly.
I'd say it's **nobody's fault**, just businesses choosing what's cheaper.
think: **Buying teams shrink** a lot, and juniors are exposed.
I want to be the one who **checks the system's orders**, not the one replaced.
do: Run a **trial** where AI drafts all orders for my range and I approve them.
Keep a **log of AI errors** to show Ingrid what I add.
Apply for buyer jobs at **bigger chains** with more of these roles.
feel: **Uneasy**, with a lot of **excitement** mixed in.
S1.quote: If I don't run the AI ordering trial, someone in head office will, and they'll do it without me.
fieldNote: She'd **automate her own range** first to stay in control of the change.
Her **centre view** means she blames no one for cost-cutting.
She worries for Ingrid (her boss), a strong **relationship buyer** who hates screens.

steps.text: Run a trial where AI drafts all orders for her range
Log every AI ordering error to show Ingrid her value
Apply for buyer roles at bigger pharmacy and beauty chains

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and nobody's ready, and I'd say it plainly without screaming. I'd want governments to sort out some kind of income support fast. Online I'd post about practical things, like how to cut costs and what skills still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job is all thinking work, emails, prices, planning, so it's gone by 2028. Being good at AI just means I see it first. My studio rent is the big thing, and five months of savings doesn't last long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now, before it arrives, I'd push the vintage shop hard and see if it could cover my rent, because selling physical clothes still needs hands. I'd ask the salons we supply whether they need someone front of house, which is people work. And I'd cut back to one streaming service and no holidays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have a plan, but it's thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the salons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know the products better than half their staff, and doing someone's skin is hands-on. Robots for that come around 2031, maybe later, because people want a person touching their face. It's three years at least, maybe more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound calm. Are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. I'm on my own, I don't have kids, my studio is cheap-ish. If I had a mortgage and a baby I'd be terrified. But I'd still be losing my main income, so I'm not pretending it's fine.

say: I'd say it's **huge** and nobody's ready, plainly, without screaming.
I'd want **income support** fast and post practical tips on cutting costs.
think: My job is all **thinking work**, so it's gone by **2028**.
Five months of savings **doesn't last long** against studio rent.
do: Push the **vintage shop** to try to cover rent.
Ask client **salons** about front-of-house or beauty work.
**Cut back** to one streaming service and no holidays.
feel: **Anxious**, with a plan she admits is **thin**.
S2.quote: Being good at AI just means I see it first.
fieldNote: Her **adaptability** doesn't protect her job, but it speeds her pivot.
She points to the **hands-on salon work** and its later robot date.
Living alone without children keeps her from **alarm**, she says.

steps.text: Grow the vintage clothes shop until it covers the studio rent
Ask client salons about front-of-house or skincare work
Cut to one streaming service and skip holidays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent warning, use it. I'd tell friends the same thing I'd tell myself: pick something that needs hands or needs people, and start now. At work I'd try to be useful in the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd get maybe three or four good years as a buyer, maybe as the person running the AI buying. Then around 2031 it's gone. But that's enough time to build something of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the wholesaler and run the AI buying as hard as I could, learning every bit of it. Evenings I'd take a beauty therapy course, a year part-time. And I'd save toward my own small skincare shop, aiming for ten thousand by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a direction. That helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A shop of your own. What would it look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small place selling Korean skincare, with treatments in the back room. I know the suppliers and I know the margins. The treatments keep it hands-on, so it lasts longer than a pure shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk you're worried about there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That everyone has the same idea. If thousands of laid-off office people open little shops, the rents go up and customers spread thin. I'd want to be early, which is why I'd start in year one, not year four.

say: I'd say **five years** is a decent warning, so **use it**.
I'd tell friends to pick work that needs **hands or people**.
think: I get three or **four good years** as a buyer, then it's gone around 2031.
That's enough time to **build something** of my own.
do: Run the **AI buying** at the wholesaler and learn every bit of it.
Take a one-year part-time **beauty therapy** course in the evenings.
Save **ten thousand** by 2030 toward my own skincare shop.
feel: **Anxious**, but with **a direction**, which helps a lot.
S3.quote: If thousands of laid-off office people open little shops, the rents go up and customers spread thin.
fieldNote: She'd turn buying knowledge into a **skincare shop** with hands-on treatments.
Her worry is **crowding**: everyone pivoting to the same idea.
The five-year gap lets her move **early**, which she values.

steps.text: Run the wholesaler's AI buying system for her range
Take a one-year part-time beauty therapy course
Save ten thousand by 2030 for her own skincare shop
Open a small Korean skincare shop with a treatment room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real gift, if people use it. I'd be the annoying friend telling everyone to plan. At work I'd be fairly relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'm in good shape. I'd have time to get really good at buying, maybe move up to Ingrid's level, and then open my shop in my early thirties. Robots doing facials by 2039 is a problem for a forty-year-old me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay and aim for a senior buyer role in three years. I'd keep growing the vintage shop and save steadily. Around 2030 I'd start planning the skincare shop for real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at most. It's the kind of future I'd quite like to be in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the economy tanks. If everyone's poorer, nobody buys forty-euro serums. That's a bigger worry for me than the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Ingrid your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eventually. She'd probably want to invest, honestly, she's talked about wanting out of corporate life. We'd make a decent team, her contacts and my systems.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a real gift, if people use it.
I'd be the friend telling everyone to **plan ahead**.
think: I'm in **good shape**: I can reach Ingrid's level, then open my shop.
**Facial robots** by 2039 are a problem for a forty-year-old me.
do: Aim for a **senior buyer** role within three years.
Keep growing the **vintage shop** and saving steadily.
Start planning the **skincare shop** for real around 2030.
feel: **Uneasy** at most, in a future she'd quite like.
S4.quote: If everyone's poorer, nobody buys forty-euro serums.
fieldNote: Her bigger fear is a **weak economy**, not robots.
She imagines partnering with Ingrid (her boss), combining **contacts and systems**.
The long warning makes her **optimistic** about her own path.

steps.text: Work toward a senior buyer role within three years
Keep growing the vintage clothes shop at weekends
Plan and fund her own skincare shop from 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my plan would be thin and my savings only last five months. What would help is cheap small-business loans and help with commercial rents, so people like me can open something real instead of competing for the same few jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what customers want. Everyone talks about what AI can do, but people still want a person to recommend a moisturiser. If customers keep wanting people, some of these jobs come back in a different shape.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about what AI can do, but people still want a person to recommend a moisturiser.
portrait: Carla is a **27-year-old junior buyer** of cosmetics from Italian and Korean factories, living alone.
She uses **AI tools daily** and sees her weak spot as judgment, after an unsold sunscreen order.
She'd **automate her own range** first in Steady Disruption, to stay in control of the change.
Her long-term plan is a **skincare shop** with hands-on treatments, built from her buying knowledge.
She ranges from **calm** to **anxious**, never alarmed, because she lives cheaply and has no children.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her plan would be thin and savings last five months.
